content: In physiology, the term serous fluid refers to various bodily fluids that are typically pale yellow, transparent, and generally benign in nature. Saliva is composed of both mucus and serous fluid. The serous component of saliva contains the enzyme amylase, which plays a critical role in the digestion of carbohydrates. The minor salivary glands of von Ebner, located on the tongue, secrete amylase. The parotid gland exclusively produces serous saliva. The other major salivary glands produce mixed saliva, which contains both serous and mucus components. Another type of serous fluid is secreted by serous membranes, also known as serosa. These are two-layered membranes that line the body cavities. The serous fluid located between the two layers of the serous membranes functions as a lubricant, reducing friction caused by muscle movement. A common characteristic of serous fluids is their involvement in facilitating processes such as digestion, excretion, and respiration. Blood serum is the liquid portion of blood that remains after clotting has occurred. As a result, it lacks clotting factors. This distinguishes blood serum from blood plasma.
